**Sūrat al-ʿAṣr (The Declining Day)**

Meccan (*makkiyyah*, revealed in Mecca), though it is said to be Medinan (*madaniyyah*, revealed in Medina). It has three verses.

[p-6249] In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words:

[1–3] ﴿By the declining day﴾ ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ ﴿except for those who believe and do righteous deeds and advise one another to truth and advise one another to patience﴾.

﴿By the declining day﴾: that is, by time (*al-dahr*). Allah the Exalted swore by it because it encompasses wondrous events, both those that remain and those that pass. For this reason it is said of it: "Father of Wonder" (*Abū al-ʿAjab*). It is also because it is mentioned along with the blessings it contains and their opposites, so it alerts a person that he is prepared for both loss and happiness. The oath by it also honors it and exalts its status, implicitly clearing it of the loss and blame attributed to it, as has been said:

*They blame time, though there is nothing blameworthy in it except those unfit for time.*

It is also permissible that by "al-ʿAṣr" is meant the known time in which the ʿAṣr prayer is obligatory.

The Imam said: It was the custom of the Arabs to gather at the time of ʿAṣr, converse, and discuss their affairs, and sometimes their talk included what is unseemly or what harms one another. So people imagined that the time itself was blameworthy. Therefore Allah swore by it to alert you that time in itself is not something to be blamed or reviled, as people have become accustomed to saying: "A cursed time," "an hour of misfortune," "an evil age," and what resembles these. Rather, it counts good things just as it counts bad things, and it is the vessel for Allah's glorious affairs of creation, provision, honor and humiliation, lowering and raising. How then could it be blamed in itself? What may be blamed is only the hateful deeds that occur in it!

﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾: that is, in loss (*khusr*), because he has squandered his capital, which is the light of the innate disposition (*fiṭrah*) and the original guidance, by preferring the worldly life and its fleeting pleasures, being veiled by them and by time, and wasting the enduring for the perishable.

﴿except for those who believe﴾: that is, in Allah and in what He has sent down of truth, with a faith that has taken possession of their wills, [p-6250] so that they act only in accordance with their beliefs, as He said: ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾. Al-Qashani said: that is, [they acquire] the virtues and goods, meaning they gain them and thus profit by an increase of the perfective light (*al-nūr al-kamālī*) over the light of receptivity (*al-nūr al-istiʿdādī*), which is their capital.

"And advise one another to truth": that is, they enjoin one another to what Allah has sent down in His Book of commands, and to avoiding what He has forbidden of disobedience. ﴿And advise one another to patience﴾: that is, to endure what Allah tests His servants with, or to remain upon truth, for reaching the truth is easy, whereas remaining upon it and being patient with it through steadfastness and striving for its sake is what manifests the authenticity and reality of faith.

Remarks:

The first: The Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in *Miftāḥ Dār al-Saʿādah*: al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "If all people contemplated this surah, it would suffice them." The explanation of this is that the stages are four, and by completing them a person attains the utmost perfection:

The first: knowing the truth. The second: acting upon it.

The third: teaching it to one who does not know it well. The fourth: being patient in learning it, acting upon it, and teaching it.

Thus Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the four stages in this surah. He swore by time in this surah that every person is in loss, except those who believe, namely those who knew the truth and affirmed it; this is one stage. And [those who] "did righteous deeds," namely those who acted upon the truth they knew; this is another. And "advised one another to truth," enjoining it upon one another by teaching and guiding; this is a third stage. ﴿And advised one another to patience﴾: they were patient upon the truth and enjoined one another to be patient with it and steadfast; this is a fourth stage.

This is the utmost perfection, for perfection is that a person be perfect in himself and perfect others. His perfection lies in reforming his two faculties, the cognitive and the practical. The reform of the cognitive faculty is by faith, and the reform of the practical faculty is by doing righteous deeds; and his perfecting of others is by teaching them, being patient with them, and enjoining them to be patient in knowledge and action. Thus this surah, despite its brevity, is among the most comprehensive surahs of the Qur'an for all good. Praise be to Allah who made His Book sufficient above everything else, a cure for every disease, and a guide to every good. End of quote.

[p-6251] The second: Al-Razi said: This surah contains a severe warning, because He, the Exalted, judged all people to be in loss except those who possess these four things: faith, righteous deeds, mutual advice to truth, and mutual advice to patience. This shows that salvation is contingent upon the totality of these matters. Just as it is obligatory for the responsible person to attain what concerns his own self, so it is obligatory for him regarding others to undertake matters such as calling to religion, sincere counsel, enjoining good and forbidding evil, and loving for his brother what he loves for himself. Then He repeated "advising one another" so that the first would include calling to Allah and the second steadfastness upon it; or the first is enjoining good and the second forbidding evil. From this is His saying: ﴿And forbid what is reprehensible and be patient over what has afflicted you﴾ [Luqman: 17]. And ʿUmar said: "May Allah have mercy on the one who points out my faults to me."

The third: Al-Razi said: The verse indicates that truth is heavy, and that trials accompany it; therefore He joined advising to patience.

The fourth: The specification of mutual advice to truth and to patience, from among their inclusion within righteous deeds, is to highlight the complete care given to these two.

The Imam said: Among those deeds is calling to truth and enjoining patience, but He intended to single out these two matters for mention, because they are the guardians of every good and the foundation of every matter. Truth is what is established of a firm reality or a sound law, and it is what is indicated by a decisive proof or by direct observation and witnessing. So the condition for salvation from loss is that people know the truth, bind their own selves to it, let it take root in their hearts, and then that people carry one another upon it, by each calling his companion to believe in the established realities over which reason does not dispute and on which transmitted proof does not differ, and by distancing themselves and others from illusions and imaginings in which souls find no rest and for which no guiding proof exists. This is not achieved except by employing thought and perfecting reflection upon the cosmos, until the soul is able to repel the false illusions that come to it. This is a release of reason from every restriction, while requiring precision in reflection, not going along with recklessness and being deceived [p-6252] by habit and fancy. Whoever does not take himself to the task of carrying people to the sound truth after he has known it, is among the losers. How much you see in this verse of the explicit text that admits no interpretation.

Patience is a strength of the soul to bear the hardship of righteous action, and to bear the hardship of losing pleasure, if attaining it would contradict truth or what the sound Law does not permit, on which there is no disagreement. It is also to bear pains when calamities befall, without anxiety and without going beyond the limits of truth and the Law in repelling them. So the condition for salvation from loss is that you be patient, that you enjoin patience upon others, and that you urge them to complete their powers with this noble virtue, which is the mother of all virtues. You cannot urge them to it until you yourself are adorned with it; otherwise you would be among those who say what they do not do. Then you would not be among those who "do righteous deeds." End of quote.

The fifth: The Imam said: He said "tawāṣaw" (they advised one another) and did not say "awṣaw" (they advised), to show that salvation from loss is attached to the eagerness of each member of the community for truth, and each one's inclination to have his people and those concerned with the matter of truth advised with it, so that he may advise his companion to seek it, being concerned that he see the truth and accept it. Thus in this forceful expression there is, as it were, an explicit statement of their mutual advice to truth and their acceptance of the counsel to it when it is directed to them.

The sixth: Ibn Kathir said: Al-Tabarani narrated through the chain of Hammad ibn Salamah, from Thabit, from Ubayd Allah ibn Hisn, who said: Two men from the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when they met, would not part until one of them recited to the other Sūrat al-ʿAṣr to its end, and then one of them would greet the other with peace. The Imam said: People thought that this was for blessing, but that is an error; it was rather so that each of them would remind his companion of what was revealed in it, especially regarding mutual advice to truth and mutual advice to patience, so that before parting one might obtain from the other a counsel of good, had it been with him.

The Imam, may Allah have mercy on him, explained this surah with a separate tafsir for which no precedent has been set. Whoever wishes to expand upon its secrets should refer to it.

[p-6248] In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
